name: Device-Related Infection (CIED / Vascular Catheter)

likely: Candida species (especially with prolonged central line dwell time, TPN)
possible: Gram-negative bacilli (less common but seen, especially with femoral lines or GI source)
pathogens.why: Device-related infections are dominated by skin-flora gram-positive organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus) that colonize the device surface and form biofilm, with Candida becoming relevant in patients with prolonged central access and risk factors such as TPN or broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure.

investigations.test: Blood cultures (peripheral and through each catheter lumen if not removed)
investigations.why: Differential time-to-positivity (catheter culture positive significantly earlier than peripheral) supports a catheter-related source.
Confirms the device as the source when growth matches blood culture results.

investigations.test: Echocardiography (if S. aureus bacteremia, prosthetic valve, or persistent bacteremia)
investigations.why: Screens for endocarditis, a serious complication of device-related bacteremia, particularly with S. aureus.

investigations.test: Repeat blood cultures after line removal/initiation of therapy
investigations.why: Confirms clearance of bacteremia, especially important for S. aureus where persistent positivity changes management significantly.

) raises concern for device-related infection. Source control (device removal/exchange where feasible) is as important as antibiotics — antibiotics alone frequently fail to clear infection while the device remains in place, particularly for biofilm-forming organisms.

clinicalPearls: CIED-related endocarditis (CIED-IE) involves either the device hardware itself or the endothelium at points of device contact, and occasionally coexists with concurrent valvular infection (Harrison 22e p.1078).

The timing of CIED-IE is split roughly into thirds: about one-third present within 3 months of implantation or manipulation, one-third between 3 and 12 months, and one-third more than a year afterward (Harrison 22e p.1078).

CIED infection can be obvious from a generator pocket infection (especially within 6 months of device manipulation) or cryptic, arising through bacteremic seeding without any visible pocket involvement (Harrison 22e p.1082).
Risk of device-associated endocarditis is reported as higher on implanted defibrillators and resynchronization devices than on permanent pacemakers (Harrison 22e p.1078).

In a patient with a CIED, an unexplained Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (and persistent coagulase-negative staphylococcal bacteremia) without another source is likely to indicate CIED-IE or valvular IE and should be investigated and managed as such (Harrison 22e p.1084).

Relapse of bloodstream infection after a course of antimicrobial therapy in a CIED patient increases the likelihood that the device is the source and warrants treatment as CIED-IE (Harrison 22e p.1084).

S. aureus device-related infections tend to be acute with both local and systemic manifestations and to progress more rapidly than the indolent course seen in non-S. aureus staphylococcal infections; a pyogenic collection at the device site is relatively common (Harrison 22e p.1200-1201).
harrison.pathophysiology: Cardiac implantable electronic devices (pacemakers, implantable defibrillators, cardiac resynchronization devices) and other prosthetic intravascular hardware provide an avascular foreign surface that organisms colonize and on which they persist. Infection localizes to the generator pocket and/or the intravascular leads, and may extend to the endothelium at points of lead contact, producing endocarditis (CIED-IE). Staphylococci dominate because skin flora is the principal portal; S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci cause the majority of CIED-IE cases. Once organisms establish on the foreign material, antimicrobial therapy alone usually fails to eradicate them, because the retained device continues to act as a nidus for persistent or recurrent infection (Harrison 22e p.1078, p.1201).
additionalDifferentials: Left-sided native-valve or prosthetic-valve endocarditis (may coexist with or be mistaken for CIED-IE) (Harrison 22e p.1078, p.1084)
Bloodstream infection from an extracardiac focus (e.g., gram-negative, streptococcal, or enterococcal bacteremia) not arising from the device (Harrison 22e p.1084)
Remote-site metastatic infection complicating bacteremic CIED infection, such as vertebral osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1084)
infectionMimics: Non-device bloodstream infection from a separate source presenting with fever and sepsis in a CIED patient (Harrison 22e p.1084)
additionalInvestigations: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): detects vegetations in >90% of patients with definite IE; an initial study may be falsely negative in a minority, so a negative TEE when IE is likely should be repeated in 7-10 days rather than used to exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1083).

Three or more separate blood culture sets (two-bottle, ~10 mL per bottle) from different venipuncture sites; if negative at 48-72 h, obtain additional sets and consult the lab for optimal techniques (Harrison 22e p.1082-1083).
FDG-PET/CT: less sensitive than TEE for intracardiac pathology in CIED-IE but useful for assessing CIED pocket and lead infection and extracardiac/remote complications (Harrison 22e p.1083).
Aspiration of any pyogenic collection at the device/pocket site, combined with blood cultures, to establish the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1201).
Echocardiographic assessment is specifically indicated in monomicrobial S. aureus bacteremia when an intracardiac device is present (Harrison 22e p.1084).
redFlags: S. aureus bacteremia in a patient with a CIED with no alternative source (Harrison 22e p.1084)
Persistent or relapsing bacteremia after antimicrobial therapy in a device patient (Harrison 22e p.1084)
Generator pocket inflammation/pyogenic collection at the device site (Harrison 22e p.1082, p.1201)
Lead vegetation >2 cm, which carries a risk of pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.1085)
harrison.prognosis: Removal of the infected CIED during the initial hospitalization is associated with increased 30-day and 1-year survival compared with antibiotic therapy and device retention. Attempted salvage of an infected device with antibiotics alone plus long-term suppressive therapy is usually unsuccessful and is reserved only for patients whose devices cannot be removed or who decline removal; left in place, the device remains a nidus for persistent or recurrent infection (Harrison 22e p.1084, p.1085, p.1201).
pitfalls: Treating an infected CIED with antibiotics alone (salvage/suppression) usually fails and should not be the default approach (Harrison 22e p.1084).
Using a negative TEE to rule out CIED-IE when clinical suspicion is high, rather than repeating the study in 7-10 days (Harrison 22e p.1083).
In critically ill patients already on antibiotics for other indications, blood cultures may be negative and device-related endocarditis missed (Harrison 22e p.1200-1201).

Assuming every bloodstream infection in a CIED patient indicates the device: gram-negative, streptococcal, or enterococcal bacteremia from an extracardiac focus may not be device-related, though relapse afterward raises suspicion for CIED-IE (Harrison 22e p.1084).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison distinguishes generator pocket infection without bacteremia (more localized) from bacteremic CIED infection and CIED-IE (more severe, with risk of coincident left-sided valve infection or remote metastatic foci); complete hardware removal is required across the spectrum of established CIED-IE and pocket or intracardiac lead infection (Harrison 22e p.1084, p.1085).
